title: V'Zot HaBerachah: an inheritance (Deuteronomy 33:4)
hook: the Torah is "the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob", learned from childhood

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' last words: blessings, tribe by tribe. Your line was end with a blessing. Today, one verse from among those blessings, the one the Talmud says a child learns first.

What's the first sentence you remember learning by heart? A nursery rhyme, a prayer at bedtime, a pledge at school, a line from a song. Whatever it was, it may still be in there, word for word. The Talmud says that when a Jewish child first begins to talk, there's a particular verse a parent should teach. It isn't from Genesis, at the beginning of everything. It's from the very end of the Torah, tucked in among Moses' blessings.
screen: `A RHYME, A PLEDGE, A SONG.` → `STILL THERE, WORD FOR WORD.` → `A CHILD'S FIRST VERSE.`

segments.voice: "Moses commanded us a law, An inheritance of the congregation of Jacob." In Hebrew: Torah tzivah lanu Moshe, morashah kehillat Ya'akov. The Talmud, in Sukkah, says that as soon as a child can speak, the father teaches him this verse, along with the first line of the Shema. Notice the little word lanu, to us. A child's first verse already says we. Now the second half. Morashah, inheritance. And whose inheritance is it? Not the priests'. Not the scholars'. The congregation of Jacob: everyone. Maimonides makes the point sharply. Israel was given three crowns, he writes. The crown of priesthood went to Aaron's family. The crown of kingship went to David's line. But the crown of Torah is set out for anyone who wants it: whoever wishes may come and take it. The Talmud also plays with the word. It reads morashah, inheritance, as if it said me'orasah, betrothed: the Torah isn't only handed down like property; it's meant to be loved. And some teachers notice that Hebrew has two words for inheritance. Yerushah is what you receive. Morashah, they suggest, is a heritage you hold in order to pass it on. Either way, the first verse a child learns says: this belongs to you, and to all of us.
screen: `TORAH TZIVAH LANU MOSHE.` · `A CHILD'S FIRST VERSE.` · `THREE CROWNS, ONE OPEN TO ALL.` · `INHERITED, AND HANDED ON.` · then, large: `INHERITANCE FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Choose a short line: this verse, if you like, Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob, or any line from these weeks that has stayed with you. Say it once, close your eyes, and say it again without looking; notice which word slips, and go back for it.
V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. And in it, morashah: an inheritance for the whole congregation.
Your line: inheritance for everyone. Whoever wishes may come and take it. Day five hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Following the Talmud, the verse 'Torah tzivah lanu Moshe' is traditionally among the first a young child learns, often sung, together with the first line of the Shema.

chat.says: Is the Torah mostly for rabbis and scholars to study?
options: The verse calls it the inheritance of the whole congregation: it's for everyone.
Mostly, yes; the crown of Torah was handed down to Aaron's family.
Yes, it was given to the kings of David's line to keep for the people.
chat.meaning: Morashah kehillat Ya'akov: an inheritance of the whole congregation. Maimonides says the crown of Torah is open to anyone who wants it.

morashah.meaning: inheritance; some read it as a heritage to pass on

Shema.meaning: the prayer whose first line a child learns early

Sukkah.meaning: a Talmud tractate; it names a child's first verse

Maimonides.meaning: a medieval scholar who taught the three crowns

sources.quoted: Moses commanded us a law, An inheritance of the congregation of Jacob.

notes: Deuteronomy 33:4 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Sukkah 42a: when a child can speak, the father teaches 'Torah tzivah lanu Moshe' and 'Shema Yisrael'. Paraphrased.
Maimonides, Talmud Torah 3:1: three crowns; the crown of Torah is 'set and ready for all Israel... whoever wishes may come and take it'. Paraphrased.
Yerushah vs morashah distinction is attributed to later commentators (often cited in the name of various modern teachers); kept as 'some teachers'.
